1.why: B is a semantically corrupted twin of D ('everything important is on there' as consent to erase). Authors usually corrupt the key's scenario to build a distractor, so the live stimulus is 'we'll have to wipe/reinstall' and D is the coherent conditional agreement.

2.why: Only option that responds to an object being presented ('is this it?'); B/C/D all pivot to a third party or another room. Weak — B (colour discrepancy) is the detail-engaging rival.

3.why: A and C are an accept/decline twin pair on the same offer ('should I stay while you finish?'); TOEFL keys take the gracious side, and C is the selfish version. B and D are off-scenario.

4.why: Three of four (A, C, D) answer a complaint rather than a general question, so the stimulus is a complaint about a used copy's download code; a price reduction is the resolution that fits a used item, D (swap for new) does not.

5.why: Only option that answers a yes/no offer ('hold it until everything's in' vs send piecemeal). B and D bounce a question back, C answers a pickup-time question nobody can have asked if the office is offering a choice.

6.why: Complaint about a machine cutting out; A is the helpful redirect. B is dismissive, C is self-contradictory ('they all cut out' vs 'that one's old'), D presumes a safety-key detail the option set never corroborates.

7.why: A, C, D are all 'the 4:40 is fine' family; B is the only option requiring the inference that 4:40 arrives too late. A is B's corrupted twin (accepts arriving at 5:10 for a 5:00 class).

8.why: The only option that reasons across two dates rather than simply granting one. D is the trap for hearing the earlier date; A and C change the subject.

9.why: A direct request ('add my name to the title slide') most naturally gets acceptance; A and B are a redirect twin pair and would each need the stimulus to establish a different owner. Genuinely uncertain — the smooth-accept shape is exactly what a repaired batch would use as bait.

10.why: Options frame an advisor recommending a different timeline. D accepts advice; A misreads it as criticism of pace, C restates a plan the advice contradicts, B asks about a detail the advice already implies.

11.why: Same shape as 16: bland-accept (D) vs arithmetic-correction (B). Applying the batch rule that the key engages a checkable detail, B. Coin-flip against D.

12.why: Stimulus is a deadline tied to travel; A commits to a specific time before it, B is the vague twin ('sometime next week'), C and D deflect into questions about the trip.

13.why: A polite refusal with a reason fits a request to be seen sooner. A echoes the stimulus's 'ten minutes' literally, which is usually the echo trap; B and C fit routine check-in stimuli instead.

14.why: All four accept 'tonight', so the discriminator is the third trial. B is the only one that closes the gap the option set keeps pointing at; C presumes all three trials already exist, A jumps to a final draft.

15.why: A and B are the smooth-accept pair; the key corrects a wrong assumption. C (wrong signer) fits a bare 'can you sign this', D requires the stimulus to have named a form colour, which is a less likely thing to say.

16.why: 1200 split three ways is 400, not 600 — the only option that checks a number rather than repeating one. D is the trap for hearing 'six hundred' and agreeing, A echoes it, B asks past it.
